docs.text: Arizona State University Robotics Engineering and Autonomous Systems Engineer: Jaedyn Harris

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome to my RAS 304 engineering project portfolio!

This website documents the research, design, and development of an Infrared-Based Cliff Detection System using the Vishay TCRT5000 reflective optical sensor.

The purpose of this project is to explore how infrared sensing technology can improve the safety and navigation of autonomous robotic systems.

Throughout this portfolio, I will document the engineering design process, including component selection, circuit calculations, system architecture, and electrical schematic development.

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
Autonomous robots rely on sensors to detect and respond to their surroundings. One important safety challenge is identifying sudden changes in floor elevation, such as stairs, ledges, and drop-offs.

Without an effective detection system, a mobile robot could travel beyond the edge of a supporting surface, potentially damaging its components.

My project focuses on designing a compact and cost-effective infrared cliff detection circuit capable of identifying the presence or absence of a nearby surface.

The system uses the TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensor, which contains both an infrared-emitting diode and a phototransistor.

docs.title: How Does Cliff Detection Work?
docs.text:
The cliff detection system operates using reflected infrared light.

  1. Infrared Emission: The infrared LED emits light toward the ground beneath the robot.

  2. Surface Reflection: When a surface is present, some infrared light reflects toward the phototransistor.

  3. Signal Detection: The phototransistor responds to the reflected light, producing an electrical signal.

  4. Cliff Identification: When the reflected light decreases below a calibrated threshold, the circuit identifies a possible drop-off.

  5. Robot Response: The detection output can be used by a robotic controller to initiate a safety response.

Design Principle: A decrease in reflected infrared light can indicate that the supporting surface is no longer present. Detection reliability depends on sensor positioning, surface reflectivity, and calibration.

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives of this project include:

  • Design an infrared-based cliff detection system.
  • Understand the electrical characteristics of the TCRT5000 sensor.
  • Calculate appropriate resistor values for the infrared LED and phototransistor circuit.
  • Develop a functional system block diagram.
  • Select components based on voltage, current, and power requirements.
  • Create a complete bill of materials (BOM).
  • Design an electrical schematic using KiCad.
  • Document engineering decisions and potential design limitations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Cliff Detection Subsystem is designed to prevent the robot from driving off elevated surfaces. It uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors connected to a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano.

The microcontroller monitors reflected infrared light from the ground and communicates potential cliff hazards to the master controller.

docs.title: Power Source
docs.text:
• 3S Li-ion battery (9–12.6 V) or 9 V bench adapter
  • J1 barrel jack
  • 750 mA fuse (proposed)
  • LM2940CT-5.0 voltage regulator
  • Regulated 5 V power supply
  • USB connection for programming and debugging

The Curiosity Nano's external power connection must be configured according to Microchip's hardware requirements.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:

Pin Function RA0 / ANA0 Left TCRT5000 analog input RA1 / ANA1 Right TCRT5000 analog input RD0 Left infrared LED control RD1 Right infrared LED control RB0 UART2 transmit (proposed) RB1 UART2 receive (proposed) GND Common ground

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
The subsystem uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors, positioned on the left and right sides of the robot.

Each sensor contains an infrared LED and phototransistor. The LED emits infrared light toward the ground, while the phototransistor detects reflected light.

The sensor outputs are read through the Curiosity Nano's analog-to-digital converter.

docs.title: Team Interfaces
docs.text:
The subsystem communicates with the master controller through Connector 4 using UART2.

The ribbon cable carries UART transmit, receive, and common ground connections. Exact connector pin assignments must be confirmed with the team.

docs.title: Functional Description
docs.text:
Power enters the subsystem through the J1 barrel jack and passes through fuse protection and a 5 V voltage regulator.

The two TCRT5000 sensors continuously monitor reflected infrared light from the ground.

The Curiosity Nano reads the sensor signals through RA0 and RA1 and compares them against calibrated thresholds.

When either sensor detects a possible loss of ground, the Curiosity Nano sends a cliff warning to the master controller through UART2.

The master controller can then command the motor subsystem to stop or change direction.

docs.title: Part 1: Component Comparison
docs.text: The purpose of the Cliff Detection subsystem is to detect when the robot approaches an edge or drop-off. Three sensors were considered based on cost, sensing capabilities, electrical requirements, and integration with the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

docs.title: 1. TCRT5000 Infrared Reflective Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $1.63

Pros: - Low-cost and readily available. - Compact design with an infrared emitter and phototransistor. - Can detect changes in reflected infrared light. - Simple analog interface with the PIC18F57Q43.

Cons: - Reflectivity changes with floor color and material. - Requires external resistors and signal conditioning. - Sensitive to sensor mounting height and alignment. - Does not directly measure distance.

View TCRT5000 on DigiKey

docs.title: 2. VL6180X-SATEL Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $22.70

Pros: - Measures physical distance rather than reflected light intensity. - Less affected by floor color. - Provides precise distance measurements. - Compact optical sensor.

Cons: - Higher cost than the TCRT5000. - Requires I2C communication. - More complex software integration. - Measurement timing must be considered.

View VL6180X-SATEL on DigiKey

docs.title: 3. VL53L0CXV0DH/1 Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $4.63

Pros: - Measures physical distance using time-of-flight technology. - Less dependent on surface reflectivity. - Compact footprint. - Supports precise distance threshold detection.

Cons: - Requires low-voltage power and compatible logic levels. - Uses I2C communication. - Requires additional software configuration. - Surface-mount package complicates assembly.

View VL53L0CXV0DH/1 on DigiKey

docs.title: Part 2A: Electrical Requirements
docs.text:
The following values were recorded in the initial component comparison.

Component Voltage Current Listed PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 3.3V / 5.0V 50 mA TCRT5000 5.0V 60 mA VL6180X-SATEL 2.8V–5.0V 19 mA VL53L0CXV0DH/1 2.8V–3.3V 19 mA

Important: The TCRT5000's 60 mA value is the infrared LED's absolute maximum continuous forward current, not its required operating current.

The sensor contains two electrically separate components: 1. Infrared LED — requires a current-limiting resistor. 2. Phototransistor — requires a sensing circuit to produce a usable output voltage.

docs.title: Selected Component: TCRT5000
docs.text:
The TCRT5000 was selected for the Cliff Detection subsystem because of its low cost, compact size, and relatively simple electrical interface.

The sensor uses an infrared LED to illuminate the floor and a phototransistor to detect reflected infrared light.

When the robot travels over a reflective surface, infrared light returns to the phototransistor. When the robot approaches an edge, the amount of reflected light decreases. The PIC18F57Q43 can monitor this change and determine whether a possible cliff is present.

Compared with the VL6180X-SATEL and VL53L0CXV0DH/1, the TCRT5000 does not require I2C communication. This simplifies integration with the microcontroller.

The primary disadvantage is sensitivity to different floor materials and colors. Testing and calibration will be required to establish reliable detection thresholds.

docs.title: Integration Plan
docs.text:
1. Supply the infrared LED through a current-limiting resistor.
  2. Connect the phototransistor to an appropriate sensing circuit.
  3. Connect the sensing circuit output to a PIC18F57Q43 ADC input.
  4. Calibrate the reflected-light threshold.
  5. Send a cliff detection signal to the robot's control system when the threshold is crossed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this power budget is to estimate the electrical power required to operate my TCRT5000 infrared cliff detection circuit.

A power budget is important because it verifies that the selected power supply can deliver sufficient current to all components without exceeding their electrical ratings.

My cliff detection system uses a TCRT5000 reflective optical sensor, consisting of an infrared LED and a phototransistor.

The calculations below estimate current consumption and power requirements for a single sensor circuit operating from a regulated 5V DC supply.

docs.title: Electrical Design Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Value Supply Voltage 5.0 V DC Sensor Vishay TCRT5000 Infrared LED Forward Voltage (Assumed) 1.25 V Target LED Current 20 mA LED Series Resistor 220 ohms Phototransistor Load Resistor (Example) 10 kohms Number of Sensors 1

Note: The resistor values and operating currents must be verified against the final KiCad schematic.

docs.title: Power Calculations
docs.text:
Electrical power is calculated using:

P = V x I

Where:

  • P = Power (Watts)
  • V = Voltage (Volts)
  • I = Current (Amperes)

docs.title: 1. Infrared LED Current
docs.text:
The infrared LED requires a series resistor to limit current.

Using Ohm's Law:

I = (Vs - Vf) / R

Where:

  • Vs = 5.0 V
  • Vf = 1.25 V
  • R = 220 ohms

I = (5.0 - 1.25) / 220

I = 0.01705 A = 17.05 mA

docs.title: 3. LED Series Resistor Power
docs.text:
P = I² x R

P = (0.01705)² x 220

P = 0.0639 W = 63.9 mW

A standard 0.25 W resistor provides adequate power dissipation capacity for this example.

docs.title: 4. Phototransistor Circuit
docs.text:
The phototransistor current depends on the amount of infrared light reflected from the surface.

Assuming a 10 kohm pull-up resistor:

Imax = V / R

Imax = 5 / 10000

Imax = 0.0005 A = 0.5 mA

This is the maximum current through the load resistor under the simplified assumption that the phototransistor is fully conducting.

docs.title: Estimated Power Budget
docs.text:
Component / Branch Voltage Current Power Infrared LED 1.25 V 17.05 mA 21.3 mW LED Series Resistor 3.75 V 17.05 mA 63.9 mW Phototransistor Load Branch (Maximum) 5 V 0.5 mA 2.5 mW Total Supply (Maximum) 5 V 17.55 mA 87.8 mW

The LED and its series resistor form one current path. Their currents must not be added together when calculating total supply current.

The estimated maximum current is:

Itotal = 17.05 + 0.5 = 17.55 mA

The estimated maximum supply power is:

Ptotal = 5 x 0.01755 = 0.0878 W

Total Estimated Power = 87.8 mW

docs.title: Design Margin
docs.text:
To provide additional capacity, a 25% design margin is applied.

Irequired = 17.55 mA x 1.25

Irequired = 21.94 mA

The 5V supply should therefore provide at least approximately 22 mA for the sensor circuit under these assumptions.

This estimate does not include any microcontroller, voltage regulator losses, indicator LEDs, or other external components.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Based on the example calculations, a single TCRT5000 cliff detection circuit is expected to consume a maximum of approximately 87.8 mW from a regulated 5V supply.

The infrared LED branch accounts for most of the power consumption, while the phototransistor sensing branch requires comparatively little current.

The calculated resistor power dissipation is within the rating of a standard 0.25 W resistor.

These results provide a preliminary estimate for power supply selection. Final values must be recalculated using the actual components and verified through circuit testing.
